title: London
alternative_titles: London: A Poem in Imitation of the Second Satire of Juvenal
description: Johnson's first published poem, a vigorous translation-of-argument of Juvenal's third satire that replaces the ancient Rome with the London of George II. The speaker Thales retires to a remote country village rather than endure the corruption, insecurity and snobbery of the capital, while Johnson's own indignation at the treatment of the poor, the Scotch immigrant and the dependent writer breaks through the Roman mask. It is the founding document of Johnson's literary career and of his lifelong quarrel with metropolitan patronage and moneyed pride.
plot_or_argument: Thales, disgusted with London, resolves to leave it and persuade his friend to join him in a rational rural retirement. The poem then catalogues the evils of the city: the insecurity of property, the tyranny of the rich over the poor, the degeneracy of the great house and its flattered heir, the corruption of the law, the theatre and the court, and the insolence of wealth in high life. Scottish poverty and the waves of immigration south are given a famous passage of indignation, and the embers of Roman jealousy of foreign arts are turned on the fashionable importation of Italian opera and Continental taste. The conclusion returns to the defence of honest poverty, the pleasures of study and the hope that verse may preserve virtue from contagion.
narrative_structure: A single sustained argument in two loosely joined movements, the invective against London and the praise of retirement, framed as a dialogue between Thales and an unnamed friend and closed by an address to the muse; the Juvenalian progression is interrupted by strongly personal passages.
principal_characters: Thales; Astrella; Licentia; Corydon; the unnamed friend and addressee
literary_form: verse satire in the Juvenalian manner, an Augustan 'imitation' rather than a literal translation
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with a heavy, polysyllabic and Latinate diction, occasional triple and dactylic rhymes, and long periodic sentences running across several couplets.
historical_context: Written after Johnson's failed schoolmastership at Market Bosworth and his London literary apprenticeship, and published in the politically charged years of Walpole's ministry, when the excise scheme of 1737 and the growing quarrel with Spain had made the rhetoric of national corruption and ministerial influence a everyday subject of debate. Its attack on corrupt wealth and on the treatment of dependents addressed the anxieties of the newly professional Grub Street letters that Pope and Swift had already mapped.
literary_significance: The poem announced Johnson as the leading satiric voice of the generation after Pope and established the moral vocabulary - independence, dependence, the dignity of poverty, suspicion of commercial splendour - that informs Rasselas and the periodical essays. Its handling of the Scottish immigrant makes it a central text for eighteenth-century writing about the nations, and its couplet practice widened the Augustan line for later moral poets.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson's authorship is documented by his own publication and by later bibliographical and copyright evidence.
bibliographical_notes: Published as a single sheet in May 1738 and revised and considerably enlarged for a second edition in the same year, to which Johnson added further satiric passages. Modern reading texts are those in the Yale edition of the Poems of Samuel Johnson (ed. John Monteath Green and Robert DeMaria, 2005).

title: A Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
alternative_titles: Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language, Humbly Submitted to the Publick by Samuel Johnson
The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
description: The prospectus and manifesto issued to launch the Dictionary, addressed nominally to the Earl of Chesterfield and the nine other booksellers who subscribed for the work. It sets out the method, the historical scope and the philosophy of a dictionary of an untreated, unauthorised modern language, and distinguishes an orthoepist, a grammatist and a critic. It is at once a working proposal, a piece of self-justification, and one of the finest occasional prose performances of the century.
plot_or_argument: Johnson argues that English has never been settled by a national academy, and that the attempt to fix a living language is in itself vain: words and meanings change with the commerce and literature of a nation. He proposes to register rather than to regulate, to collect the vocabulary from the best writers within a limited historical period, and to illustrate each word with quotations that both authenticate the sense and preserve the literary record. The Plan reviews previous English and Continental lexicons, defends the division of labour he has contracted for with the booksellers, and closes with a frank claim to have carried the work through without patronal assistance.
narrative_structure: A continuous epistolary essay: dedication to Chesterfield, historical account of previous dictionaries and of the absence of an English academy, statement of method and of the three provinces of the lexicographer, and a personal peroration on the conditions of authorship.
literary_form: printed prospectus and critical dissertation in formal balanced prose
meter_and_prosody: Prose; periodic sentences of Latinate weight, tricolon and balanced clause, in the manner of the attached dedication; no verse.
historical_context: Issued in 1747 after the booksellers of London had contracted with Johnson for a dictionary on the model of the French Academy's, in the same decade as the repeated but failed projects for an English academy and the debate over ascertaining the language that Swift had opened in 1712. The subscription and copyright economy of the trade, and the example of the French and Italian lexicons, set the terms of the proposal.
literary_significance: The Plan is the foundational statement of English philological self-consciousness, replacing the dream of an academy with the authority of usage and the evidence of quotations, a practice that still governs historical lexicons. Its frank account of the economics of authorship makes it a key document for the professionalisation of letters, and its closing pages were long read as the manifesto of independent labour.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested, though the Plan was written under contract and in the shadow of a booksellers' subscription list; the coolness of Chesterfield, which Johnson recorded in the letter of 1755, belongs to the later correspondence rather than to this document.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in folio by J. and R. Tonson in 1747, with the dedication to Chesterfield; reprinted as the front matter of the first edition of the Dictionary in 1755 and in various modern selections, including the Yale edition of the Dictionary on the Internet and in print.

title: The Vanity of Human Wishes
alternative_titles: The Vanity of Human Wishes: The Tenth Satire of Juvenal Imitated
description: Johnson's greatest poem, an imitation of Juvenal's tenth satire on the emptiness of human desire, transposed from Roman invective into a Christian meditation on providence. Its catalogue of disappointed wishes - the scholar, the statesman, the general, the great man, the beauty, the aged - moves from the fall of Sejanus to the quiet exemplary death of the virtuous widow. The poem replaces the satirist's confidence in exposure with the recognition that only prayer and resignation remain.
plot_or_argument: The speaker invites History to reveal the disasters produced by human hope, surveying ambition in learning, in public office, in arms and at court, and showing that each wish, granted or refused, destroys the wisher. The celebrated Sejanus passage enacts the sudden collapse of a favourite's power, and the fall of Wolsey gives the argument a distinctly modern and Christian dimension. The portraits of the beauty and of the aged wretch extend the miseries of the body and of dependence, and the poem ends by surrendering choice to providence in the prayer for wisdom that closes Johnson's verse.
narrative_structure: A single invective movement organised as a series of exemplary portraits after the manner of the satire, framed by an invocation and closed by a devotional turn to prayer and wisdom; the examples accumulate rather than develop.
principal_characters: The speaker; Sejanus; Wolsey; the beauty; the aged wretch; the virtuous widow; History
literary_form: verse satire and meditative poem in the Juvenalian tradition, with a strong native elegiac and devotional undertone
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, famously varied by dactylic and trisyllabic substitutions that give the line an unusual weight; the couplet is often enjambed and the antithesis strained to the breaking point.
historical_context: Published on 28 January 1749 from Johnson's lodgings in Gough Square in the same season as the opening of his periodical labour; the fate of ministers and favourites was a live topic after the fall of Walpole and the recent rising of '45 made the instability of power and the misery of civil war immediate experience.
literary_significance: It is generally held to be the finest poem Johnson wrote and one of the major moral poems of the century, matching Pope's Essay on Man with a darker and more Scriptural account of desire. Its Sejanus and its closing widow supplied later poets with a model of the meditative satiric couplet, and the poem stands at the centre of the preromantic interest in melancholy, mutability and resignation.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson described the poem in his own correspondence and it was published under his name.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for J. and R. Tonson in quarto in 1749 and reprinted in the collection of Johnson's poems of 1755; standard text in the Yale edition of the Poems of Samuel Johnson (2005). Johnson's title-page describes the work as an imitation of the tenth satire of Juvenal.

title: The Rambler
alternative_titles: The Rambler, by Samuel Johnson, Late of Pembroke College in Oxford (series title)
description: The twice-weekly periodical of moral essays that Johnson wrote almost single-handedly between 1750 and 1752, in the tradition of the Tatler and the Spectator but with a severer, more introspective and more explicitly Christian purpose. Under the persona of a detached observer of life, Johnson examined marriage, friendship, learning, sorrow, death, self-deceit and the conduct of the passions. Its 208 numbers, many reprinted in book form in the author's lifetime, made him the most influential moral writer of his generation.
plot_or_argument: Each number treats one moral or psychological question, usually opening with a general proposition and proceeding through examples, cases of life and a closing application. Recurring arguments include the danger of self-flattery, the miseries of domestic life, the obligations of patience and resignation, the vanity of worldly success, and the necessity of examining one's own conduct; a small body of narrative and allegorical papers, and some tales and oriental fictions, carry the lessons in story. The persona of the Rambler - an unattached spectator travelling and observing - allows a tone of melancholy detachment that is quite unlike Addison's sociability.
narrative_structure: A serial essay periodical of 208 twice-weekly numbers issued from January 1750 to March 1752 and collected in volumes during Johnson's lifetime; individual papers are self-contained, ordered loosely by subject, and framed by a running persona and by occasional letters from correspondents.
principal_characters: The Rambler; the correspondents and cited examples; occasional narrative personae (the prudent husband, the unhappy pair, the hermit of the Oriental tales)
literary_form: periodical moral essay, with embedded tales, allegory and criticism
meter_and_prosody: Prose; long balanced periods of Latinate syntax, sententious parallelism and repeated emphasis, forming the most deliberate and most imitated example of Johnson's 'pump' style.
historical_context: Launched in the generation after the great Spectator and Tatler papers, during the rapid expansion of provincial and suburban reading and of the periodical market. Johnson wrote most of the numbers himself and at great speed, with small documented help from friends, and the twice-weekly half-sheet format kept him on a permanent deadline.
literary_significance: The Rambler redefined the periodical essay from a instrument of politeness into an instrument of moral and religious self-examination, and its sales and long book-life established the essay serial as a vehicle of serious thought. Johnson's style here became a byword and a target for the whole century, and several numbers anticipate the arguments of Rasselas and the later criticism.
attribution_notes: Substantially Johnson's own work; a small number of contributions associated with Elizabeth Johnson, Thomas Tyrwhitt and Mrs Hester Thrale are separately recorded in the Yale edition and are not claimed for particular numbers here.
bibliographical_notes: Issued twice weekly in folio half-sheets from January 1750 to March 1752 and collected in volumes during the eighteenth century with Johnson's revisions; the standard scholarly text is that of the Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson, which records the disputed attributions.

title: A Dictionary of the English Language
alternative_titles: A Dictionary of the English Language, in Which the Words are Derived from the Originals, and Illustrated in Their Different Significations by Examples from the Best Writers (first edition title)
Johnson's Dictionary
description: The two folio volumes that settled the lexicography of English for half a century and remained the standard authority until the Oxford English Dictionary. Johnson gave some 42,773 words and illustrated their senses with a vast body of literary quotations, treating the language as a national literature rather than as a set of logical terms. The work was performed largely by Johnson's own labour, assisted by a small body of clerks, on the booksellers' contract signed in 1747.
plot_or_argument: Each entry gives the orthography, the etymology where it can be traced, the parts of speech and the senses arranged from the primary to the derived, each authenticated by a quotation from an approved writer. Johnson's discussions of the difficulty of fixing a living language, of the limits of etymology and of the treatment of low or indecent words are recorded in the Grammar and the Plan prefixed to the volumes, and the illustrative citations - Shakespeare, Milton, Dryden, Pope and hundreds more - amount to an anthology of English writing.
narrative_structure: A reference work: an alphabetical macrostructure, preceded by the Plan and a Grammar of the English tongue; no narrative order, but a strict microstructure of word, etymology, senses, examples.
literary_form: two-volume folio dictionary with a prefixed grammar and prospectus; lexicographical and philological writing
meter_and_prosody: Prose of extreme compression in the definitions, with the illustrative quotations supplying the rhythm and the authority; the Grammar is written in the same periodic style as the Plan.
historical_context: Produced in the decade after Chesterfield's indifference to projects for an English academy and in the same years as the Rambler papers; the booksellers' share system, the labour of the six copying clerks and Johnson's lodging in Gough Square provide the physical conditions of the work, and the Seven Years' War had already begun when it was published.
literary_significance: It established quotation-as-evidence, the historical treatment of senses and the idea that a dictionary is a record of a literature, all of which passed into later lexicons; it also created the modern image of the independent professional writer. Its definitions remain a literary document, and the work is a central text for eighteenth-century theories of language, usage and national letters.
attribution_notes: Johnson is the author of the whole design and of the definitions; the clerks and later bibliographers assisted the execution, and the etymologies relied on the philology then available, including Junius, Skinner and Tooke's predecessors.
bibliographical_notes: Published on 7 April 1755 in two folio volumes by a consortium of London booksellers, with the Plan and a Grammar prefixed; a second edition followed in 1755-56 and a revised fourth edition in 1773, to which Johnson supplied his Preface. The standard scholarly discussion is the Yale edition of the Dictionary and the digitised facsimiles of the first edition.

title: Letter to the Earl of Chesterfield
alternative_titles: Letter to the Right Honourable Philip Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield, 7 February 1755
Johnson's Letter to Chesterfield
description: The brief reply that closed Johnson's nine years of expectation of patronage, sent days before the publication of the Dictionary after Chesterfield had revived his acquaintance at its approach. Its courteous refusal - that favour is unwelcome when it comes 'delayed till I am indifferent, and cannot enjoy it; till I am obstinate, and cannot repay it' - is the most celebrated letter in English literary history and the classic statement of the independent professional writer. It was copied, circulated and printed soon after and became part of the lore of letters.
plot_or_argument: Johnson recounts how he first approached Chesterfield nine years earlier, was repulsed, and nonetheless worked on without help; he observes that the Earl has now thought it convenient to remember him, and declines the favour on the ground that it comes too late to be welcome. He insists that he has needed no patron and will owe no obligations he cannot repay, and closes with a wish for the Earl's happiness that is decorously but unmistakably cold. The argument is not a personal quarrel but a claim about the dignity and self-sufficiency of learned labour.
narrative_structure: A single brief formal letter of a few short paragraphs, ordered chronologically through the history of the acquaintance and rhetorically from courtesy to refusal to the closing wish.
principal_characters: Samuel Johnson; Philip Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield
literary_form: familiar letter in the state paper manner; epistolary prose of the Augustan school
meter_and_prosody: Prose, balanced and judicial in cadence, moving from ironic gratitude to the famous refusal that favour arrives 'delayed till I am indifferent, and cannot enjoy it; till I am obstinate, and cannot repay it', and ending with a decorately cold wish for the Earl's happiness.
historical_context: Written in the week before the Dictionary was issued, when the subscription and copyright economy of bookselling had already made the old aristocratic patronage relation embarrassing to both parties; Chesterfield's own letters to his son had publicly recommended a very different model of literary dependence.
literary_significance: The letter fixed the image of authorship against patronage for the next century and supplied the standard anecdote of Johnson's independence. It is a touchstone for the history of the literary marketplace, and its rhetoric has been read as the perfect example of the period's controlled, judicial prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the letter is documented by Johnson's holograph copies and by early print, though no holograph of the final version survives.
bibliographical_notes: Dated 7 February 1755. It circulated in manuscript immediately and was printed in periodicals and in collections of letters within the year, though the exact first appearance in print is not asserted here; the text is standardly read from the Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson.

title: The Idler
alternative_titles: The Idler, by the Author of The Rambler (series title)
description: Johnson's second periodical paper, a weekly series of short essays contributed to a London newspaper between 1758 and 1760 and afterwards collected. Its persona - a man who has resolved to do nothing and to write only what comes to him - lets Johnson examine idleness, attention, marriage, reading, hopes and fears with a lighter, more playful touch than the Rambler, while still turning each subject to moral account. The 104 papers include some of his best brief criticism and his wryest analysis of self-deceit.
plot_or_argument: Each paper takes a single topic - the danger of sloth, the pleasure of novel-reading, the conduct of life in easy circumstances, the use of criticism, the fears of the ignorant, the duty of parents and children - and pursues it by definition, example and epigram rather than by sustained argument. The framing personae of the Idler and of his club of loungers supply a comic distance from the matter, and several numbers advertise Johnson's own habits and quarrels. The series repeatedly insists that idleness is itself a labour of the mind and that the unexamined life of ease is the most dangerous of all.
narrative_structure: A serial periodical of 104 weekly papers, first issued from 1758 within a newspaper and later gathered in volumes; the numbers are free-standing, with only a slight continuity of personae.
principal_characters: The Idler; the members of his club; the correspondents of the occasional papers
literary_form: periodical essay and character-writing in the Spectator tradition
meter_and_prosody: Prose; shorter and less Ciceronian periods than the Rambler, with a pointed conversational sententiousness that Johnson himself thought more readable.
historical_context: Written in the same years as the Dictionary and the Rambler, for a new newspaper venture that needed established hands; Johnson's authorship was recommended by the reputation of the Rambler and his papers were read as a continuation of the Addison-Steele serial, from which they differ by their scepticism about politeness.
literary_significance: The Idler consolidated the essay serial as a vehicle for criticism as well as morals, and the numbers on Shakespeare, on the pleasure of reading and on the vanity of expectations are among the most quoted of Johnson's shorter prose. In a lighter register it carries out the same analysis of dependence and self-knowledge that makes the Rambler serious.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the Yale edition records the very few papers doubtfully assigned to other hands.
bibliographical_notes: Contributed weekly to a London newspaper from 1758 and collected in volumes during the eighteenth century with Johnson's revisions; the standard scholarly text is the Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson.

title: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia
alternative_titles: Rasselas
description: Johnson's philosophical tale, the briefest and most widely read of his works, in which a prince of Abyssinia escapes from the Happy Valley to try the possible forms of life and finds none sufficient. Its fable of choice - the inspection of marriage, trade, public life, religion, retirement and country solitude - is delivered in a style of proverbial compression. It was composed for a purpose Johnson's friends recorded and was published without his name on the title-page.
plot_or_argument: Rasselas, secured in the Happy Valley among princes kept from the succession, flees with his sister Nekayah and the poet Imlac to see the world. They examine the conditions of happiness in turn - the court and its favours, the town and its commerce, marriage and the family, the country life, the scholar's solitude, the religious house - and each proves disappointed by jealousy, idleness, avarice or sorrow. The closing chapters assemble the travellers to report their conclusions and leave the choice of life undecided, commending instead the inquiry itself and the knowledge of human limits.
narrative_structure: A short tale in 46 brief chapters: the escape from the Happy Valley, a middle sequence of experiments of life, and a closing symposium of reported conclusions, with little incident and much general reflection.
principal_characters: Rasselas; Nekayah; Imlac; the keepers of the Happy Valley; the hermit of the earlier chapters; Pekuah
literary_form: philosophical tale in the Oriental-fiction manner, drawing on early modern travel narrative
meter_and_prosody: Prose; balanced, abstract and strongly periodic, closer to the Rambler than to the novelistic manner of his contemporaries, with dialogue carried in sententious exchange.
historical_context: Composed at the end of the 1750s, when Johnson was occupied with the Dictionary and the Idler papers and had recently suffered his mother's death; the Abyssinian setting draws on travel accounts of Ethiopia current in translation, and the tale's analysis of choice belongs to a decade of speculative fiction from Voltaire to the Scottish moralists.
literary_significance: Rasselas is the classic English example of the experiment-of-life tale and the standard literary statement of Johnson's doctrine that happiness cannot be found by choice alone; its Happy Valley became one of the most allusive places in English letters. Its treatment of religion, of suicide and of the inequality of conditions made it a work on which later readers tested their own opinions.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson's authorship was known among his friends and asserted in later editions, while the speed and occasion of composition are reported at second hand, so the composition dates here are approximate.
bibliographical_notes: Published anonymously in two volumes in 1759, the copyright being Johnson's to dispose of; the traditional account of a very brief composition derives from Boswell. The standard text is that of the Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson.

title: Preface to Shakespeare
alternative_titles: Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare
Preface, containing an Account of the Observations and Corrections of the Editor
description: The general preface to Johnson's eight-volume edition of Shakespeare, the most influential piece of dramatic criticism of the eighteenth century. It defends Shakespeare as the poet of nature against the neoclassical rules, answers the charge of violating the unities, and grounds the pleasure of tragedy in the audience's real rather than imaginary credulity. The critical essay is attached to an editor's account of his own method and of his predecessors.
plot_or_argument: Johnson first justifies the editorial work, defending his emendations and censuring the laxity or rash conjecture of earlier editors. He then argues that Shakespeare's primary merit is his just representation of universal nature and of individual human character, so that his dramas serve as a mirror of life. Against the rules he urges that the unities of time and place are not required by nature but by an arbitrary conception of the spectator's belief, since the audience knows it is in a theatre and is moved by real passions excited by fictitious events. He catalogues Shakespeare's faults - far-fetched language, quibbles, the mixture of tragic and comic scenes, inattention to moral teaching - and concludes that even his errors proceed from the abundance of his observations of life.
narrative_structure: A two-part preface: an editorial defence of the method used in the edition, followed by a critical essay on Shakespeare's excellences, the rules and the unities, the faults, and the closing assessment, the argument built through cases and instances rather than by system.
principal_characters: Shakespeare; Rymer; Theobald; Pope; Warburton; Thomas Otway; Addison
literary_form: critical preface and dissertation attached to a scholarly edition; prefatory commentary and literary criticism
meter_and_prosody: Prose; the plainest and most direct of Johnson's styles, still periodic and balanced but without the Rambler's weight, with a famous sententious cadence in the closing paragraphs.
historical_context: Written for the edition contracted after the Dictionary and the Rambler, in the same years as Garrick's regenerated Shakespearean performances at Drury Lane and the antiquarian editorial labours of Theobald, Warburton and Pope; the debate over the unities and over Shakespeare's regularity had filled English criticism since Rymer and Dennis.
literary_significance: The Preface is the decisive transfer of Shakespeare from the charge of barbaric irregularity to the defence of nature and general truth, and its analysis of theatrical belief remains a starting point for the aesthetics of drama. It established the model of the critical preface to a scholarly edition, and much later argument about character, plot and the rules has been conducted in the terms it set.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested, though the edition was a collaborative book: the editorial assistance of Thomas Tyrwhitt, and Johnson's own account of that help, are documented in later letters.
bibliographical_notes: Published as the front matter of The Plays of Shakespeare, 8 volumes, 1765, with a revised second edition in 1773; the Preface is standardly read in the Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson and in collections of eighteenth-century Shakespeare criticism.

title: Taxation Tyrannical; or, The Colonies and Britain Compared
alternative_titles: Taxation Tyrannical: or, The Colonies and Britain Compared, in Answer to a Pamphlet entitled Taxation No Tyranny
description: Johnson's last and fiercest political pamphlet, written at the crisis of the American dispute as a reply to the anonymous Taxation no Tyranny and to the colonial claim that representation is necessary to lawful taxation. It argues that authority rather than consent is the ground of government, that the colonies are subordinate parts of an empire maintained at the cost of the whole, and that the language of liberty used by the planters covers the interest of slavers. Its invective against the slave trade is the most quoted passage in the pamphlet and among the strongest in Johnson's prose.
plot_or_argument: Johnson denies the doctrine that taxation without representation is tyranny, urging that no part of a community can be exempt from the burdens of the whole and that the ties of empire are not dissolved by distance. He compares the condition of the colonists with that of Britain, insists on the expense and risk incurred for the colonies, and predicts that a claimed independence would produce only a republic of planters and a new scene of revolt. Against the colonial assertion of the rights of Englishmen he sets the treatment of their own slaves, asking why the loudest yelps for liberty should come from the drivers of negroes, and closes with an unapologetic defence of the authority of the mother country.
narrative_structure: A short polemic in continuous argument: statement of the question, refutation of the doctrine of representation, comparison of colonies and mother country, and a peroration of indignation against colonial inconsistency.
principal_characters: The anonymous author of Taxation no Tyranny (conventionally identified as Josiah Tucker, Dean of Gloucester); the American assemblies and their leaders; the planter and his slaves
literary_form: political pamphlet and polemical answer in the Augustan tractate manner
meter_and_prosody: Prose; rapid and indignant, heavy with rhetorical question, amplification and stark antithesis, the style of the late political tractates rather than of the periodical essays.
historical_context: Written after the destruction of the tea at Boston and before the outbreak of war, when Johnson, aged and ill, took the ministerial side in a cause many of his friends favoured, in a pamphlet war that included repeated colonial declarations and Burke's conciliatory policy. His protest against the slave trade belongs to a longer engagement with slavery that includes the arguments with Boswell.
literary_significance: The pamphlet is the classic tory answer to the American case, and its exposure of the hypocrisy of slaveholding revolutionaries made it a durable text in the literature of abolition as well as in the history of political argument. It closes Johnson's career as a public writer and remains a touchstone in debates about authority, consent and empire.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson's authorship is documented by his correspondence and by Boswell, while the authorship of the pamphlet answered rests on a conjecture long current among bibliographers.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1775 and reprinted among Johnson's political tractates and in the Yale Edition of the Works; the title-page names the adversary only as the author of Taxation no Tyranny, and the pamphlet is standardly read alongside Burke and the colonial declarations of the same years.

title: Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect
alternative_titles: The Kilmarnock Volume
Kilmarnock Poems
description: Burns's first volume, printed by subscription at Kilmarnock in 1786 and the event that made him at once the most talked-of poet in Scotland. It gathers the tales and dramatic pieces, the elegies and addresses, the verse epistles to friends and brothers, and the songs, most of them in the Scottish dialect and in the stanzaic tradition inherited from Ramsay and Fergusson. The volume is a self-consciously provincial and labouring man's book, furnished with an advertisement to the subscriber and a glossary of Scots words.
plot_or_argument: The collection moves between the Ayrshire world of ploughing, courtship, tavern and communion field, and the moral and elegiac registers of the addresses and laments. Its satirical pieces expose Presbyterian hypocrisy, rural quackery and the arrogance of rank, while the epistles build a community of friends, brothers and patrons about the poet. Throughout, the volume pleads for the dignity of the Scottish vernacular and of untaught genius, a claim made explicitly in the advertisement and in the poems on national character and song.
narrative_structure: A subscription volume ordered by the author into classes of piece - tales, addresses, elegies, epistles, songs - with an advertisement, a list of subscribers and a glossary of Scots terms, rather than a single sequential design.
principal_characters: Luath and Caesar; the cotter's family; Death and Doctor Hornbook; the ploughman-speaker of the addresses; the friends and brothers of the epistles
literary_form: collected poems: Scots tales, fables, verse epistles, elegies, addresses and songs, with prefatory advertisement and glossary
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly stanzaic Scots in the six-line Habbie and rambling measures inherited from Ramsay, with songs to current airs, ballad stanzas, and a few pieces in conventional English prosody.
historical_context: Produced while Burns was preparing to emigrate to a overseer's post in Jamaica after the failure of his Nithsdale farming scheme, and the success of the volume rescued him from that plan; it stands in the line of Allan Ramsay's The Ever Green and the Tea-Table Miscellany, of Fergusson's Edinburgh poems, and of Herd's collections of Scottish songs, and appeared in the full tide of the Scottish Enlightenment's institutional life in Edinburgh and Glasgow.
literary_significance: The Kilmarnock volume is the foundation text of modern Scottish literature and the moment at which the vernacular revival of Ramsay and Fergusson was converted into a national poetry of observation, sympathy and satire. Its publication created the literary cult of Burns and remains a classic instance of subscription authorship in the provincial book trade.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Burns controlled the volume, its advertisement and its glossary, though several pieces adapt earlier printed and manuscript sources, a practice he recorded in his later musical and poetic collections.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by John Wilson at Kilmarnock in 1786 for the author by subscription, in an edition of some 612 copies. A greatly enlarged second edition was issued at Edinburgh in 1787, dedicated to the nobility and gentry of the Caledonian Hunt, adding poems and revising others; per this batch's convention that Edinburgh issue is described here and not entered as a separate record, and Burns's dialect texts are given original_language Scots.

title: The Cotter's Saturday Night
alternative_titles: The Cotter's Saturday Night. In Imitation of Spence
description: Burns's most cherished poem, a picture of the Sabbath evening of an Ayrshire cottager's family, composed in November 1785 and first printed in the Kilmarnock volume. The scene of family worship, with the father reading and expounding and the mother ordering both the devotions and the supper, is rendered with an accuracy that made the poem the standard image of Scottish domestic Presbyterianism. It closes with addresses to the poet's rustic muse and to his native country that turn the cottage scene into a declaration of poetic and national allegiance.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the household from the day's work finished to the assembling of the family, the call to worship, the reading of scripture with plain homely expounding, the singing of a paraphrase, the father's discourse on the religion of the heart, and the simple meal. The mother appears as the practical head of the household's piety and economy, the daughters at their work, and the old grandfather remembering the covenanting past. The closing stanzas withdraw from the scene to set the honest poverty of the cotter against the empty splendour of rank, and to ask that Scotland itself be the poet's theme.
narrative_structure: A continuous descriptive-didactic poem in several grouped stanzas, opening with a short invocation, passing through the hours of the evening in order, and ending in an apostrophe to the muse and to native Scotland.
principal_characters: The cottager father; his wife, the mother of the family; the daughters and sons; the grandfather of the former times
literary_form: descriptive and moral poem in the Scottish vernacular, in the domestic-picture tradition imitated from Spence as the subtitle indicates
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic Scots in alternating four- and three-beat lines with a close-running rhyme, in the old Scottish narrative manner inherited from Ramsay and Fergusson; the invocation and the closing addresses use the same measure.
historical_context: Written at Mossgiel in the hardest years of Burns's farming, out of a household scene he knew exactly, and shaped by the eighteenth-century cult of honest poverty and domestic piety as well as by Fergusson's dialect pictures of Edinburgh life. Its Presbyterian Sabbath subject matter belonged to a culture of family worship, paraphrase singing and covenanting memory still vivid in Ayrshire.
literary_significance: It became the emblematic poem of Scottish domestic and religious life, among the most reprinted, quoted and illustrated texts in the language, and was taken from Francis Jeffrey onward as the instance of genius nourished by home scenes. Its representation of family worship also makes it a document for the social history of Presbyterianism and for the sentimental celebration of rural poverty.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Burns recorded the poem in his own memorandum of dates and discussed its dialect and its models in his literary correspondence. The identification of the Spence named in the subtitle remains a matter of comment and is not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in November 1785 and first printed in the Kilmarnock Poems of 1786, reprinted in the enlarged Edinburgh issue of 1787 and standard ever since. The text is now read from the scholarly editions of Burns's poetry and from his own annotated copies; per this batch's convention original_language is entered as Scots.

title: To a Mouse
alternative_titles: To a Mouse, On Turning Her up in Her Nest with the Plough, November, 1785
description: The shortest and most quoted of Burns's ploughman poems, addressed to a field mouse whose nest has been laid bare by the poet's plough in November 1785. Pity for the small creature turns into a meditation on provision, fear and the human lot, since the mouse at least lives in the present while mankind is tormented by memory and forecast. It is the classic lyric instance of the eighteenth-century cult of sympathy extended to the lower creation.
plot_or_argument: The speaker apologises to the frightened mouse for the destruction of its winter house, and reflects that its pains in storing for the winter have been laid aside by an accident it could not foresee. He then envies it, because its troubles are but of the moment, whereas man looks backward and forward and is wretched. The poem ends in a prayer that the mouse may be spared the cruel human remembrances, and that its fate may teach the poet himself to bear his own disappointments of hope.
narrative_structure: Six short stanzas moving from the immediate incident to apology, comparison and general conclusion, the argument of the meditation rising steadily out of a single act of ploughing.
principal_characters: The mouse; the ploughman-speaker
literary_form: occasional meditative lyric and address, in the tradition of the 'To a' poems of the Scottish vernacular
meter_and_prosody: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie): four four-beat Scots lines and two short trimming lines, with the rhyming pattern a-a-a-b-a-b and an insistent colloquial rhythm.
historical_context: Written at Mossgiel in the autumn of 1785, when Burns's farming prospects were failing and his poems were being prepared for the press; the mood of disappointed hope and of dependence on the weather of a small farm belongs exactly to that season, and the poem's ethic of pity for animals draws on the contemporary debate about sympathy and the moral sense.
literary_significance: Its lines on the best laid schemes of mice and men passing often ago became among the most familiar proverbs in English, and the poem is a standard example of the preromantic lyric that reasons outward from a small accident of feeling. It also fixed the figure of the thinking ploughman as a poet of sensibility and of providential anxiety.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is Burns's own, entered in his memorandum of the poem, and the printed title carries that date.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the Kilmarnock Poems of 1786 and reprinted in the Edinburgh issue of 1787. The standard text is that of the scholarly editions of Burns's poems; per this batch's convention the dialect original_language is entered as Scots.

title: The Holy Fair
description: Burns's great comic survey of a Church of Scotland communion preaching in the open air, in which the religious solemnity of the Holy Fair is matched against the thronging, drinking, courting and quarrelling of the field. The poem frames the scene as the vision of a ploughman homeward on a moonlit night, and lets three personae of the fair - religion, interest and fancy - contend for the meaning of what he has seen. It is the most complete poetic record of Scottish communion-season culture and one of the most sustained satires of enthusiasm in the century.
plot_or_argument: The poet, riding homeward at moonlight, recalls the scene of the preaching: the crowd spread over the braes, the preacher working the auditors with the terrors of the law and the glories of the gospel, the professional religionists scanning each other for signs of grace, and the young people making their own business of the day. The allegorical voices of Religion, Interest and Fancy then dispute the event, Religion pleading for the seriousness of the doctrine, Interest for its worldly uses, and Fancy for the human spectacle of appetite and mirth. The poem closes with the ploughman's sober re-entry into common life, leaving the value of the fair undecided.
narrative_structure: A framed narrative: a moonlit opening scene with the ploughman, the long descriptive middle on the preaching and the crowd, an allegorical tripartite dispute, and a brief closing retirement of the spectator.
principal_characters: The ploughman-speaker; the preacher of the sermon; the sitters of the audit; Religion, Interest and Fancy as speaking abstractions; the courting country folk
literary_form: comic-descriptive tale-poem with allegorical debate, in the Scottish rambling tradition of Ramsay's Christ's Kirk
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic Scots in long running measures of four- and three-beat lines with a brisk rhyme and much colloquial idiom, adapted to the tune known as Cherry and Cream; the allegorical sections keep the same narrative pace.
historical_context: Rooted in the communion preachings of the Ayrshire and Scottish west, seasonal events that drew thousands to the fields and were notorious for their profane diversions, and in the contemporary debate about enthusiasm, Methodist and evangelical preaching and the suspicion of religious enthusiasm. Burns's own experience of the revival at Kirkoswald and his acquaintance with the lay preaching of the period give the poem its technical accuracy.
literary_significance: It supplies the classic literary account of the Scottish communion season and remains a primary source for the social history of Scottish popular religion. Its mixture of dialect realism, allegory and comic detachment made it a landmark of the preromantic interest in vernacular popular spectacle, and its portraits of the preacher and of the audit of grace have become standard.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Burns revised the poem across editions and his authorship of the earlier and later states of the text is documented in his correspondence and memoranda. The precise date of first composition is not fixed, and the range entered here follows the usual scholarly reckoning.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the Kilmarnock Poems of 1786, reprinted and revised in the Edinburgh issue of 1787 and in later editions with Burns's substantive alterations. Per this batch's convention the dialect original_language is entered as Scots.

title: Address to the Deil
alternative_titles: Address to Satan
description: Burns's burlesque invocation of the Devil, an audacious piece of dialect blasphemy which treats the powers of darkness as a subject for comic natural history. The Deil is addressed as the old hags, books and superstitions have made him, and the poem runs through his titles, his habits, his attendants and his theological credentials with a humour that leaves Calvinist demonology exposed as folklore. It is at once a lampoon of priestcraft and a display of the whole vocabulary of Scottish witch-belief.
plot_or_argument: The speaker greets the Deil with mock ceremony, cataloguing his appellations, his dominion, his court and his trade in souls. He reviews the scriptures and the traditions that make the Devil a prince of this world, then deflates them with homely instances from witch stories, kirk-yard hauntings and the delusions of old women and of arguing divines. The poem's movement is from grand invocation to ridicule, ending with a wish that the poet's wit may serve to laugh the power of the devil out of the honest mind.
narrative_structure: A single sustained apostrophe organised as a catalogue - names, titles, retinue, works - with the burlesque pressure building stanza on stanza rather than through narrative incident.
principal_characters: The Deil; the speaker; the witches, divines and old wives of the alluded folklore
literary_form: burlesque verse address and satire in the Scottish dialect, in the lampooning tradition of Burns's religious satire
meter_and_prosody: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie), with its four long and two short Scots lines, giving the invective a brisk comic gait.
historical_context: Written in the middle years of the 1780s in an Ayrshire still dense with witch and ghost belief, and against a background of Calvinist teaching on Satan and of the century's learned demonology; it belongs with Death and Doctor Hornbook and Holy Willie's Prayer to Burns's campaign against priestcraft, superstition and cant.
literary_significance: The poem is the most complete poetical exploitation of Scottish demonological vocabulary and one of the boldest burlesques of religious horror in British verse, standing with the Scottish witch tradition as a document of belief and unbelief. Its handling of the Habbie stanza for sustained comic invective also made it a model for later vernacular parody.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem survives in many states and revisions of Burns's own hand, and the bibliographical record distinguishes the shorter and later expanded texts. Because the several versions were printed at different dates, the year of first publication is not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in 1785 and transmitted in several states of text; the earlier shorter version and the later expanded version were printed at different dates among the Kilmarnock, Edinburgh and Glasgow issues of Burns's poems, and the year of the first appearance in print is not asserted here, so publication_date is left null. Per this batch's convention original_language is entered as Scots.

title: Death and Doctor Hornbook
description: Burns's rollicking dialogue-poem of Death and the parish schoolmaster-doctor, a personal pamphlet against Peter Buchan, the Tarbolton excisier and poet who had insulted him in print. Death comes to drag the quack Hornbook to his trial, and the schoolmaster protests his useful ignorance of theology till the summons is served. The poem converts a local quarrel into a full-scale comic debate of the Death and the Doctor type, and a satire on pedantic presumption.
plot_or_argument: Death, in the homeliest terms, rouses the doctor from his bed to answer for his misdeeds, and the schoolmaster protests that he was never taught to fear such visitors and that his learning has been of the bookish and useless kind. The two dispute the merits of learning, of practice and of preparation for the hour of death, with the doctor's excuses running out as Death presses the account. The dialogue ends with the parson's discomfiture and with an author's appeal to common sense against the pretensions of the professional neighbour.
narrative_structure: A two-voice debate poem in continuous dialogue, opening with Death's arrival, sustaining the exchange of summons and excuse, and closing with a direct address of the poet to his adversary.
principal_characters: Death; Doctor Hornbook (a portrait of Peter Buchan); the poet-speaker of the argument
literary_form: debate poem and personal satire in the popular 'Death and the Doctor' dialogue tradition
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic Scots in the rambling six-line measures of the old Scottish comic narrative, with colloquial idiom, internal rhyme and a running dialogue of matched speeches.
historical_context: Written in 1784 as a reply to Buchan's The Farmer's Ingle, which had caricatured Burns and his friends, and thus belongs to the local literary quarrels of Tarbolton and Mauchline; at the same time it works in a folk tradition of Death-dialogues and in the eighteenth-century contempt for the quack and the small pedant.
literary_significance: It is the best example of Burns's power to turn private pique into durable poetry, and one of the liveliest surviving instances of the Death-and-doctor debate in British verse. Its portrait of the schoolmaster-poaster has become a standard document for the history of the parish school and of rural self-education.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the quarrel with Buchan and the poem's occasion are documented by Burns's correspondence and by the rival pamphlets, and the identification of Hornbook with Buchan is accepted in the standard editions.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in 1784 and first printed in the Kilmarnock Poems of 1786, reprinted with revisions in the Edinburgh issue of 1787. Buchan's The Farmer's Ingle, which provoked the poem, belongs to the same local print culture. Per this batch's convention original_language is entered as Scots.

title: The Twa Dogs
alternative_titles: The Twa Dogs. A Tale
description: Burns's animal fable of the two dogs - Luath the farmer's working stock-dog and Caesar the gentleman's pampered spaniel - who meet at a tavern door and compare the conditions of their lives. Under the covering of the beasts the poem delivers a searching social analysis of rank, idleness, hire and hunger in the agricultural west of Scotland, and one of the sharpest indictments of the privileges of great families in the century. It is among Burns's earliest considerable poems and the first open declaration of his egalitarian creed.
plot_or_argument: Caesar, kept warm and idle by his laird, and Luath, the working dog of a farmer, meet and dispute their respective happiness. Caesar reports the luxuries and the boredom of the hall, the squire's dogs, horses and flatterers, and the uselessness of his own life, while Luath describes the labour, the weather, the hunger and the honest dependence of the poor. The dialogue arrives at the poem's famous conclusion that the rank of the creature makes no difference in its worth, and that the poor dog and the poor man have at least the merit of usefulness.
narrative_structure: A framed tavern scene followed by a matched dialogue of the two dogs, each speech elaborating the conditions of its master, closing with the moral of the fable.
principal_characters: Luath; Caesar; the poor laird; the farmer and his bailiff; the tavern company
literary_form: beast fable and debate poem in the Scottish vernacular, in the tradition of Ramsay's and Dryden's dialogues of creatures
meter_and_prosody: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie), four long and two short Scots lines with the a-a-a-b-a-b rhyme, used for sustained dialogue.
historical_context: Begun about 1784 and revised for the Kilmarnock volume, in a decade of enclosure, of improving agriculture and of depressed rural wages in Ayrshire; the poem's comparison of the idle and the useful draws on a long native tradition of estates criticism and on the contemporary debate about the condition of the labouring poor.
literary_significance: It established Burns's characteristic politics of the worth of the common creature and supplied the imaginative ground of his later songs on rank and equality. As a dialect fable it is the most successful modern descendant of the Scots 'Makkar' tradition of talk between beasts, and it remains a standard text for the literature of the nations and for social analysis in verse.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Burns dated the poem in his own memoranda as an early attempt, and the standard editions record his successive revisions of the text.
bibliographical_notes: Composed about 1784 and revised for first print in the Kilmarnock Poems of 1786, with later edition variants recorded in the scholarly texts. Per this batch's convention original_language is entered as Scots.

title: Tam o' Shanter
alternative_titles: Tam o' Shanter. A Tale
description: Burns's narrative masterpiece, a tale of the farmer Tam who, leaving a fair at Alloway after drink, sees the witches and warlocks dancing by the haunted kirk and is pursued across the Auld Brig by the ghastly band, losing his mare's tail at the keystone. Written in 1790 to accompany a drawing of Alloway Kirk for Grose's antiquarian series, it moves from tavern realism to supernatural panic and back to homely commentary in a single sweep. It is the most perfectly timed comic poem in Scottish verse.
plot_or_argument: Tam's day of market, his supper with friends and his drunken ride home at moonlight are set at length, with the county's characters and pleasures named. At the kirk he watches the dance of the witches and of the Devil with his tarred tail, and, crying out in admiration at the sight, is discovered; the horde pursue him, and he escapes across the Auld Brig because a witch has no power over running water. The poem ends with the loss of Meg's tail, with Tam's shrift before his wife, and with the poet's own homely closing commentary, which deflates the horror he has just raised.
narrative_structure: A single continuous narrative in four recognisable movements - the market and tavern scene, the ride and the vision at the kirk, the pursuit, and the closing commentary - with the tonal registers of realism, terror and comedy sharply opposed.
principal_characters: Tam o' Shanter; Kate, his wife; Souter Johnnie; Nansie, Johnnie's wife; the Devil and the witch band; Meg the grey mare
literary_form: comic-gothic tale poem in the Scottish vernacular, written to illustrate an antiquarian drawing of Alloway
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic heroic couplets in Scots, broken at the crisis into triplets of fourteen-syllable alexandrine lines for the dance and the pursuit, the formal swell carrying the poem's terror and its comedy.
historical_context: Composed in 1790 at Burns's own request to supply a poem to Francis Grose's engraved series of Scottish antiquities, and thus directly tied to the antiquarian interest in kirk, brigs and witch-traditions; the witchlore of Ayrshire, the Kirk sessions' records and the popular belief in second sight supply its matter, and the poem quickly entered both printed and sung tradition.
literary_significance: It is generally held to be the greatest Scottish narrative poem and the supreme example of Burns's command of dialect, of tonal switch and of the antic machinery of belief. Its mixture of gothic terror and homely comedy makes it a central text for the literature of the supernatural in the 1790s, and its stanzaic and couplet technique was widely imitated in vernacular verse.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the circumstances of commission are documented by Burns's letters and by the account of his friendship with Grose, and the poem's text was revised by him in later printings.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in 1790 and first printed in 1791 in association with Grose's antiquarian series on Scotland, and reprinted thereafter in the collections of Burns's poems, including the edition of Dr James Currie's 1800 collection; the date of composition is deliberately recorded here although it falls just after the nominal closing year of the installment.

title: A Red, Red Rose
alternative_titles: O my Luve's like a red, red rose
description: Burns's song of enduring affection, two brief stanzas of departure and of the vow to return, which became the most familiar love lyric in Scottish and one of the most set, translated and quoted poems in English. Its opening compares the beloved to the red rose and the melody, and its closing pledge of return across the widest distance gives the whole its pathos. Burns entered it among the songs he was collecting and reworking for Johnson's musical collection.
plot_or_argument: The speaker likens his love to the newly blown rose and to the tune that strikes the ear, states the certainty of love beyond measure, and then faces the distance of parting. The second stanza pledges the return across the farthest seas and mountains till all the world be changed, closing with the image of the rivers and the sea that makes the promise seem at once impossible and certain.
narrative_structure: Two short stanzas of song, the first of comparison and present joy, the second of parting and the vow of return, with no narrative development beyond the single address.
principal_characters: The loving speaker; the absent beloved
literary_form: song lyric written for a Scottish air, in the collecting and adapting practice of the Scots Musical Museum
meter_and_prosody: Short ballad-like song stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines, adapted to the air's phrasing, with simple diction and a single sustained simile.
historical_context: Composed in the mid-1790s during Burns's last years in Dumfries, while he was contributing hundreds of songs and notes to Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, and drawing on traditional Scottish openings of the 'rose' and 'melodie' type. The song belongs to the great project of recovery and reissue of Scottish song that made the 1790s a decade of national anthology.
literary_significance: It is the most widely known of Burns's songs in English translation and setting, and a standard instance of how the antiquarian song-collecting of the 1790s produced original lyric. Its treatment of love and distance supplied a repertoire of phrase and image that passed into popular song generally.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Burns's song reworks and re-voices older traditional material, as he himself recorded in the notes to the collection, so the record of authorship should be read together with his practice of collecting and adaptation.
bibliographical_notes: Entered by Burns among the songs supplied for Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, the volumes of which were issued seriatim over the years 1787 onwards; the exact year of the first impression is not asserted here, so publication_date is left null. Per this batch's convention the lightly dialectal English of this song is entered as English, while the strongly Scots poems are entered as Scots.

title: Auld Lang Syne
description: The song of old acquaintance and of remembrance, in which the pairs of friends who have run the world together ask whether the times of 'auld lang syne' shall be forgotten. Burns presented it to Johnson as a recovered old song rather than as an invention, and his own stanzas gave the traditional phrase its enduring form. It has since become the most performed commemorative song in the English-speaking world.
plot_or_argument: The speaker proposes that the partners in former merriness should drink a cup of kindness yet for the sake of the old days, recalling the runs over the braes and the talks before they were parted by years and distance. The refrain insists on the phrase itself, converting a drinking song's occasion into a general meditation on memory, friendship and the passage of time, and closing with the pledge of remembrance.
narrative_structure: A strophic song with a fixed refrain, each verse adding a remembered scene to the toast, the argument carried by the return of the phrase auld lang syne.
principal_characters: The speaker and the old friend or friends toasted
literary_form: song lyric in the Scottish vernacular, collected and reworked from traditional material for a musical anthology
meter_and_prosody: Ballad stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines with a refrain, set to the air Burns associated with the words; the diction is plain and the syntax colloquial.
historical_context: Sent by Burns to Johnson in 1793 with a letter describing it as taken down from an old man's recitation and as belonging to the store of ancient Scottish song; the phrase and title had already been used by Allan Ramsay, and Burns's work is an act of recovery and revision within the collecting culture of the Scottish Musical Museum.
literary_significance: It is the most widely performed and most universally recognised song in the language, and the exemplar of the way Burns's collecting practice could make an old phrase into a new poem. It also stands as a document of the 1790s effort to define a national song repertory against imported opera and English popular air.
attribution_notes: Attribution to Burns is uncontested for the familiar text, but the song is expressly a recovery and reworking of earlier traditional verse, and the standard editions record the anterior phrase and Ramsay's use of the title; the composition date follows Burns's letter to Johnson.
bibliographical_notes: Contributed to Johnson's Scots Musical Museum (volumes issued from 1787 onward); the year of the first impression is not asserted here, so publication_date is left null. Per this batch's convention original_language is entered as Scots.

title: Scots Wha Hae
alternative_titles: Scots, wha hae wi' Wallace bled
Song: Scots wha hae
description: Burns's war-song written in the voice of Bruce addressing his men before Bannockburn, and the most powerful political lyric of the 1790s in Scotland. Under the cover of the fourteenth-century battle it speaks the language of liberty and of servile dependence in the present, and its challenge - who will be a slave, who a freeman - made publishers hesitate to print it anonymously as an old song. It is the classic instance of Burns turning national history into a democratic battle hymn.
plot_or_argument: Bruce calls on the Scots who bled with Wallace to remember the days that made their names, and sets the tyrant's hirelings against the freemen who fight for their own land. The song demands the choice of slavery or liberty in the strictest terms, promises the reward of victory and the shame of the slave, and ends with the call to share the battle and its prize. The historical speaker makes the contemporary application unmistakable without naming it.
narrative_structure: A short strophic song in the persona of Bruce, each stanza advancing the exhortation from memory of Wallace to the present choice, the threat of the tyrant, and the final rally.
principal_characters: Robert the Bruce; the Scots host; Edward of England as the tyrant; Wallace as the remembered leader
literary_form: persona song and war lyric set to a traditional march air, in the national-song mode of the 1790s
meter_and_prosody: Four-beat Scots lines in short stanzas with a strong march rhythm, adapted to the air of Bruce's March; the diction is imperious and monosyllabic, with the refrain-like closing address.
historical_context: Composed in the summer of 1793, in the excitement and repression that followed the French Revolution and the trials of the king, when Burns's radical sympathies were constrained by his office in the excise, to which he had been appointed in 1789; it was contributed to Johnson's musical collection as a song of the northern nation, and its publication raised the question of political offence.
literary_significance: It became one of the national songs of Scotland and a standard text of the literature of liberty, admired for its concentration and for its way of making medieval history speak to contemporary radicalism. Its use as a battle and commemorative hymn, and its place in the song repertory of the nations, make it a central document of the 1790s bardic revival.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is fixed by Burns's own letter to Johnson in the summer of 1793, and the printing of the song in the musical collection is documented, though the volumes' issue dates have been variously reckoned.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in the summer of 1793 and printed in the volume of Johnson's Scots Musical Museum that is usually dated to that year; the issue dates of the Museum volumes are bibliographically disputed, so the date of first impression follows the standard reckoning. Per this batch's convention original_language is entered as Scots, and Burns's presentation of the song in the dress of old national verse is noted here.

title: A Man's a Man for A' That
alternative_titles: For A' That, and A' That
description: Burns's democratic anthem, which asserts that rank, ribbons and titles are nothing against the worth of the honest man, and that the true aristocracy is that of virtue and character. The song gathers the language of the 1790s radical argument about precedence and desert into a strophic hymn of equality, closing with the prophecy of a day when the brotherhood of man shall be more than a phrase. It is the most quoted of all verses on human equality in Scottish.
plot_or_argument: The speaker catalogues the marks of worldly distinction - the coat of arms, the livery, the belt and the star, the flattery of menials - and insists that none of them makes the man better than his poor neighbour. The independent mind, poor and unpatented, is declared the true nobility, and the external rendings of rank are set against the worth of the upright heart. The final stanza looks forward to the coming time when man shall be a brother to man for a' that, turning the song's invective into a promise.
narrative_structure: A strophic argument in the manner of a song, each verse restating and intensifying the proposition of the refrain, ending with the prophetic closing stanza.
principal_characters: The upright poor man; the hireling and slave of rank; the 'rulers' and 'wrigglers' of precedence
literary_form: song lyric and political hymn in the Scottish vernacular, in the radical verse tradition of the 1790s
meter_and_prosody: Four-beat Scots stanzas with the burden-like return of the phrase a man's a man for a' that, adapted to an air; the diction is colloquial, abrupt and full of monosyllables.
historical_context: Written in the later Dumfries years, when the repressive measures following the French war and the agitation over parliamentary reform sharpened the language of rank and desert in Scotland; the song belongs to the same 1790s argument as the Address to the Deil and Tam o' Shanter in its contempt for precedence and for the trappings of nobility.
literary_significance: It has become the standard lyrical statement of human equality in the language, quoted at inaugurations, funerals and political meetings, and a touchstone for the history of democratic sentiment. Its union of vernacular song with a political proposition makes it a central text of the literature of the nations in the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is variously assigned by the biographers within the last years of Burns's life, and the song was not printed in his lifetime, so the composition range entered here is deliberately broad and publication_date is left null.
bibliographical_notes: Long known only in manuscript and first printed among the posthumous collections of Burns's works, the standard modern text being that of the scholarly editions of his poems and songs; the year of the first impression is not asserted here. Per this batch's convention original_language is entered as Scots.

title: Olney Hymns
description: The hymn-book prepared jointly by William Cowper and John Newton for the Olney congregation, Newton supplying the public devotional verse and Cowper the poems of inward experience. Its several divisions serve social worship, private worship and the dispensations of providence, and its most lasting contribution is Cowper's sequence of hymns of fear, desertion and assurance. The volume stands beside Watts and the Wesleys as a foundation text of Evangelical and Nonconformist hymnody.
plot_or_argument: The hymns move through the ordinary apparatus of Evangelical worship - praise, confession, prayer for grace, the conflicts of conscience, the comforts of providence and the hope of heaven - with the division devoted to private spiritual trial much of which Cowper left unfinished. His best hymns in the book, including God of my life, to thee I call and O for a closer walk with God, give the collection its enduring power, while Newton's contributions carry its narrative of redemption and mercy.
narrative_structure: A hymnal in several divisions ordered by the occasions of worship rather than by continuous argument, the parts assigned between the two authors and the whole framed by their Olney practice.
literary_form: congregational hymnal and devotional verse collection with scriptural and doxological headings
meter_and_prosody: The common, proper and long measures of English hymn metre, mostly alternating four- and three-beat iambic lines with simple rhyme, written to be sung to current tunes.
historical_context: Prepared during Cowper's residence at Olney under Newton's curacy and after his own conversion, in the household of the Morants; the book belongs to the Evangelical revival's programme of hymn-making for ordinary congregations and to the Olney custom of a full service of prayer and praise.
literary_significance: It is one of the standard sources of English hymnody and the first public proof of Cowper's devotional gift, anticipating the religious passages of the Task. Its treatment of spiritual trial and assurance makes it a primary document of Evangelical religious feeling in the later eighteenth century.
attribution_notes: The volume is expressly a joint work of Cowper and Newton and the divisions are assigned between them in the standard accounts; the printing history of individual hymns, including that usually identified as Amazing Grace, has been variously stated, so no particular first printing is asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1773 as a single volume, Cowper's share being left incomplete; later editions and the facsimiles, together with the scholarly edition of Cowper's works, record the history of the texts. The authors are entered as a pair in the relationship map, John Newton being the co-author of the whole book.

title: Poems (Cowper)
alternative_titles: Poems by William Cowper, of the Inner Temple, Esq.
description: Cowper's first collected volume, published in 1782 after long years of religious depression, retirement at Olney and work on the hymn-book, and the book that established his reputation. It gathers the didactic and meditative essays in verse, the addresses and reflections, the short elegies and the two familiar pieces Conversation and Retirement. The volume announces the temper of all his later work: reliance on providence, the praise of home, and the honesty of an unpatronised writer.
plot_or_argument: The poems argue in turn against the errors of the world and on the claims of hope, moderation and charity, and record the writer's religious experience, his mourning for the dead and his contentment in domestic retirement. Conversation and Retirement examine the fashionable round and the temptation to flee from it, setting the pattern of the blank-verse essays that culminate in the Task.
narrative_structure: A collected volume of separate poems ordered by class rather than by sequence, the blank-verse meditations and the couplet essays distributed across the book with short devotional pieces and elegies.
principal_characters: The retired poet-speaker; the fashionable world of the card-table and the great room; the friends of the Olney and St Albans households
literary_form: collected didactic, meditative and familiar verse, combining blank-verse essay poems with couplet satires and short hymns or elegies
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets heavier and more Latinate than Pope's, together with meditative blank verse of the Thomson school in the two familiar pieces.
historical_context: Published in the year that closes Cowper's first period of composition and opens his partnership with the Unwin household, after the Olney hymn project and in a season of revived interest in Thomson. Its appearance belongs to the retail book trade of the 1780s rather than to patronage.
literary_significance: The volume created Cowper's standing and made the Task possible, and its criticism of fashionable conversation and its praise of rural retirement fixed the themes for which he is read. It is a central text of the culture of feeling and of the religious verse of the Evangelical revival.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poems were composed over nearly two decades and several pieces cannot be dated precisely within that span, so the composition range entered here is approximate and follows the usual biographical reckoning.
bibliographical_notes: Issued in London in 1782 under the author's name; the standard modern text is that of the scholarly edition of Cowper's Poems, which records the first printings of the separate pieces. This volume is not to be confused with the 1785 collection that contains the Task.

title: Conversation
description: Cowper's first blank-verse essay poem, a gentle satire on the fashionable round of society written in the manner of Thomson's Castle of Indolence. Its speaker surveys the card-tables, the assemblies and the small talk of the great, and finds the whole machinery of politeness a study in emptiness and affectation. The poem is the opening movement of Cowper's long argument with the world that continues in Retirement and the Task.
plot_or_argument: Addressed to a friend who proposes a day of company, the poem describes in order the scenes of fashionable intercourse - the thronged assembly of the great room, the card table, the opera and the playhouse, the talebearer and the prude - and shows each producing its own bored and envious characters. The satire closes not in despair but in a plea for conversation that is civil, instructive and cheerful, and for the society of a few chosen friends over the noise of many.
narrative_structure: A familiar epistle in continuous blank verse, organised as a sequence of social scenes united by the addressing speaker's comments rather than by incident.
principal_characters: The advising speaker; the man of the world; the prude and the scandal-monger of the great room
literary_form: didactic-satiric familiar essay in verse, in the Thomsonian blank-verse manner
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of Thomson's school, with a colloquial ease, occasional couplet-like closures and much enjambement.
historical_context: Written late in Cowper's Olney and early St Albans period and printed with the Poems of 1782, in a decade when the manners of the ton were a staple of periodical and novelistic satire; its Thomsonian manner reflects the revived esteem for the author of The Castle of Indolence.
literary_significance: It establishes the characteristic Cowperian voice - domestic, moral, mildly ironic, strongly opposed to the metropolitan world of display - and supplies the prosodic model for the Task. Its treatment of politeness makes it a useful document for the eighteenth-century debate on the codes of conduct.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition rests on the biographical reckoning of Cowper's letters and on his own account of the poems of this period.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the Poems of 1782 and reprinted with the later collections; the standard text is that of the scholarly edition of Cowper's Poems.

title: The Task: A Poem
alternative_titles: The Task
The Task, in Six Books
description: Cowper's principal poem, a blank-verse meditation in six books that begins as an occasional exercise on a sofa and becomes a survey of retirement, of the times, of the world and of the winter year. Its movement from domestic ease to public prophecy, and its account of the Christian's dependence on providence, made it one of the most read long poems of the last third of the century. It contains the century's most quoted plea for solitary escape and some of its earliest verse protest against the slave trade.
plot_or_argument: Book I excuses the trivial occasion of the poem and commences the praise of soft retirement; Book II, the Time-Piece, moralises the hours of the day and the vanity of fashionable occupations; Book III considers the world and its corruption; Book IV the winter evening with its lamp, its tea and its news; Book V the winter morning walk in the country; and Book VI the winter walk at noon, ending in the wish for a lodge in some vast wilderness and in a religious conclusion on the faith that sustains the solitary soul.
