Throughout, the poem argues that true happiness is found in dependence on providence rather than in the noise of the age.
narrative_structure: A long poem in six books of unequal length, each opening with an address and proceeding by reflection, description and digression; the design is associational, with the winter sequence of the last three books giving the strongest local unity.
principal_characters: The retired poet; the friends and patroness of the Unwin household; the world and its votaries; the personified Times and Solitude
literary_form: meditative and didactic long poem in blank verse, in the Thomson-Ossian tradition of the reflective essay-poem
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of unusual smoothness and variety, with the famous 'O for a lodge in some vast wilderness' lines in a mixed and more prosaic measure; the couplet is used only occasionally and the sentence-periods are long.
historical_context: Written at the Olney and Weston Underwood retirements in 1783-84 on a wager or request that he should make a poem in blank verse on an unfashionable subject, and published in 1785; its reflections on the times respond to the American war's aftermath, to enthusiasm in religion, and to the growth of luxury, commerce and colonial exploitation.
literary_significance: The Task was a bestseller and the model for a generation of reflective and topographical verse, admired by Wordsworth and the younger romantics for its command of blank verse and its treatment of ordinary domestic life. Its abolitionist passage and its 'time and tide' morality made it a site of both moral and literary authority in the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Cowper's own letters and memoranda record the commission and the books' composition, and the several revisions of the text across editions are documented in the standard edition.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1785 in quarto, issued with Table Talk and the other poems of that collection; reprinted many times in the eighteenth century and standardly read from the scholarly edition of Cowper's Poems, which records the edition-by-edition revision.

title: Table Talk
description: Cowper's discursive blank-verse poem on society, reading and taste, published with the Task in 1785 and much admired by Hazlitt. Its subject is the talk of the table itself - the pleasures of conversation, the choice of books, the study of one's own company and the criticism of the literature of the day - treated with an ease that had been Thomson's before him. The poem is the most explicit statement of Cowper's beliefs about taste, retirement and the uses of letters.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens on the advantages of social intercourse and of the well-ordered table, then turns to the love of reading, the choice of the old writers against the modern scramble for novelty, and the necessity of solitude within company. Its central argument is that a man should think for himself at the table as in the study, that friendship and domestic happiness refine rather than dull the mind, and that the critic's first duty is to the plain honest sense of the writer he reads.
narrative_structure: A single continuous meditation in several marked divisions, moving by association from conversation to reading, to retirement and to literary criticism, without narrative incident.
principal_characters: The speaking friend at table; the company of readers; the modern writers of the day, unnamed
literary_form: discursive essay in verse on taste and society, in the line of the Augustan art-poem renewed by Thomson
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, the smoothest and most colloquial of Cowper's blank verse, with long sentence-periods and a marked caesural poise.
historical_context: Published in 1785 with the Task, in the season of the great vogue of the familiar essay and of the debate about reading, novelty and the book trade; its praise of the older native writers is a protest against the hurry of fashionable taste in the same years as Blair's lectures on rhetoric.
literary_significance: Later readers, Hazlitt among them, have prized it as the most accomplished of Cowper's shorter poems, and its remarks on reading and originality belong to the century's theory of taste. It also displays the blank-verse style that the romantic poets inherited from Thomson through Cowper.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is not fixed with certainty within the years before publication, and the composition start is therefore left null with the range indicated by the printing date.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1785 in the collection issued with the Task and reprinted in the successive collected editions; the text is standardly read from the scholarly edition of Cowper's Poems.

title: Tirocinium
alternative_titles: Tirocinium; or, Advice to Parents on the Point of Sending Their Sons to Public Schools
description: Cowper's poem of advice to parents on the education of their children, urging home and day-school teaching against the boarding public school. It sets the school-boy's loneliness, the tyranny of his seniors and the hardness of classical drudgery against the supervision of a father and the example of a Christian household, and extends its argument to the education of daughters. The poem is the most vigorous poetical statement of the eighteenth-century attack on the boarding-school.
plot_or_argument: The speaker urges parents to keep their sons at home, arguing that the public boarding school exposes childhood to fear, vice and an idle learning of words rather than of sense. He describes the boy's first day at school, the austerities of the seminary, the return home with its spoiled affections, and the mischief of friendships formed under such confinement. The close passes to the education of girls and to the plea that the domestic and religious instruction of the family is the true seminary of the mind.
narrative_structure: A continuous didactic argument in several thematic sections, opening with the direct advice to parents, proceeding through the picture of school life, and closing with the extension to female education and the commendation of home.
principal_characters: The advising speaker; the parent addressed; the school-boy of the description; the masters and ushers of the seminary
literary_form: didactic poem and conduct piece in blank verse, belonging to the century's writing on education and domestic duty
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of the Task's school, more abrupt and hortatory than Cowper's meditative verse, with pointed sententious closures.
historical_context: Written in 1784, when the boarding public school was already a target of moral and educational writers and when the debate over classical curriculum, parental authority and the religious training of children was active in Evangelical and dissenting households; Cowper's own schooling and its hardships lie behind the picture.
literary_significance: It is the strongest poetical intervention in the eighteenth-century quarrel over boarding, and its appeal to the domestic and imaginative life of childhood belongs with the growing cult of the child that leads to the Romantic poets. Its influence on later conduct and educational writing was considerable, and it remains a primary document for the social history of schooling.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is given in Cowper's own account, while the year of first separate impression has been variously reported, so publication_date is left null with the uncertainty stated.
bibliographical_notes: Written in 1784 and first printed separately soon afterwards, the two datings current in the bibliographies being 1784 and 1785; it is standardly read from the scholarly edition of Cowper's Poems, where the first issue is described.

title: The Castaway
description: Cowper's shortest and starkest poem, founded on the wreck of an East Indiaman in which one seaman, described as deranged, was said to have been lost, and turning the incident into a figure of the poet's own spiritual exposure. The speaker watches the thoughtless crew about their business while the abandoned man lies at the mast foot, and the wreck becomes an image of the soul for whom no pity and no hope remain. It is the most intense of the preromantic lyrics of desolation.
plot_or_argument: The poem reports the wreck, the crew's exertions and the fate of the abandoned seaman who, past reason and past hope, was left to the sea. The speaker then draws the moral likeness: he too is exposed without pity, without prayer and without the sympathies that keep others from despair. The closing stanzas refuse consolation, identifying the castaway with a man abandoned both of God and man, and leave the figure of the storming sea as the poem's last image.
narrative_structure: A brief narrative in short stanzas, passing from the reported wreck to the meditative identification of the speaker with the castaway and ending without consolation.
principal_characters: The lost seaman; the surviving crew; the meditative speaker
literary_form: meditative lyric on an occurrent disaster, in the graveyard-school manner of gloom and self-analysis
meter_and_prosody: Ballad-like stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines with a solemn rhyme, the measure giving the poem its hymn-like severity.
historical_context: Written in January 1785 on the news of the loss of an East Indiaman eastward, in the same months in which Cowper's religious depression was returning; the wreck lies near the centre of the decade's interest in maritime disaster, providence and the limits of sympathy.
literary_significance: It is the poem by which Cowper is most often read as a precursor of Romantic despair, and one of the strongest lyrics of abandonment in English. Its identification of a public news-item with private spiritual state makes it a document of the culture of feeling and of the graveyard meditation.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is fixed by Cowper's own letter, and the year usually given for the first printing is 1786, a reckoning followed here with the qualification recorded in the bibliographical note.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in January 1785 and first printed in 1786, the poem being subsequently included in the collected editions; the standard text is that of the scholarly edition of Cowper's Poems.

title: Bohoursky
description: Cowper's late war elegy on a Russian general killed in the storming of Ochakov, a short poem that turns a printed notice of a stranger's death into a meditation on honour, pity and the cost of arms. It mourns the fallen commander as a brave and humane soldier and sets the horrors of a stormed town against the praise of the man who died in the breach. It is characteristic of Cowper's last decade in its mixture of northern romantic colour and Christian regret.
plot_or_argument: The poem recalls the general's conduct and courage, the storm of the place and his death in the attack, and then asks what glory can mean for a Christian who must count the slain. It dwells on the spectacle of the field and the breach, on the pity that survives the battlefield, and on the uncertainty of fame, closing with the sense that the warrior's reward is a mourned name rather than a triumph.
narrative_structure: A brief epitaphic meditation in continuous stanzas, moving from the notice of the death to the description of the assault and to the reflection on honour and pity.
principal_characters: The Russian general Bohoursky; the assailants and defenders of the town; the mediating poet
literary_form: war elegy and occasional meditative poem, in the Ossianising manner of the late century
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic iambic verse of Cowper's late manner, with a solemn slow movement and much monosyllabic weight.
historical_context: Written in 1789 on the printed accounts of the Russo-Turkish war and the storming of Ochakov, at the close of a decade in which Cowper was deeply interested in the news of Europe and in the morality of war; his late poems on the Russian campaigns and on the French Revolution belong to the same journalistic and providential imagination.
literary_significance: It is the best of Cowper's short war poems and a useful instance of how the 1790s made a remote general's death an occasion of Christian pity, an argument later central to the literature of war. Its handling of printed report into reflection shows the late topographical voice turned to contemporary history.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem's occasion is the printed account of the Russian general's death in the Russo-Turkish war, and its date rests on the printing of 1789.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1789 in a London periodical and included in the later collections of Cowper's poems; the particulars of the periodical in which it appeared are recorded in the scholarly edition of his poetical works.

title: Account of Corsica
alternative_titles: An Account of Corsica, with Journal of a Tour to That Island, and Memoirs of Pascal Paoli
description: Boswell's travel book and political plea for the island he had visited twice, a journal of tour joined to an account of the Corsican constitution and a life of its leader Pascal Paoli. It made Corsica a cause romantique of the British reading public and helped to bring Paoli's name and the island's struggle for liberty into European debate. It is at once a work of travel narrative and an argument for the rights of a small nation against conquest.
plot_or_argument: Boswell narrates his journeys through the island, its coasts, mountains and towns, and its people's hospitality, courage and poverty, and then passes to a description of the government, the laws and the military resistance to Genoa. His memoir of Paoli presents the general as a philosopher-soldier and a model of republican virtue. The book closes in an appeal to Britain's interest and honour, urging that the Corsicans' defence of their liberty deserved support rather than indifference.
narrative_structure: A composite work: narrative journal of the tour, historical and political account of the island and its constitution, and biographical memoir of Paoli, unified by the writer's personal presence and his argument for Corsican liberty.
principal_characters: James Boswell; Pascal Paoli; the Corsican peasants and soldiers; the Genoese and the French
literary_form: travel narrative with historical and biographical matter; political advocacy in the form of a book of travels
meter_and_prosody: Prose; brisk, talkative and directly personal, with the journal's immediacy and the essayistic expansiveness of the political sections.
historical_context: Written after Boswell's visits of the mid-1760s, when Corsica had thrown off Genoese rule and was negotiating its defence against France, and when British public opinion was being mobilised by the pamphlets of the 'Corsican' party and by the project of an academy and a constitution. It belongs to the literature of European sympathy for small nations in the age of the American and Corsican causes.
literary_significance: It created the Corsican vogue in Britain, fed the wider European argument about the island's liberty in which Rousseau's projected constitution also belonged, and became a document for the history of romantic nationalism and of the cult of liberty. It established Boswell's literary identity in advance of the Life of Johnson, and it is a central text for the literature of the nations outside England.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Boswell's journeys and his acquaintance with Paoli are documented in his own journals and letters, and the book's composition follows immediately upon the diplomatic activity of the later 1760s.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1769 and reprinted several times within the decade, with translations following; the text is standardly read from the scholarly editions of Boswell's works and from his own journal materials.

title: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides
alternative_titles: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, with Samuel Johnson
description: Boswell's account of the 1773 journey with Johnson to the western islands of Scotland, kept as a day-by-day journal and withheld from print for twelve years. It records the conversation, the arguments on Jacobite memory, religion, slavery and the worth of an island life, and the scenery of Skye and Mull, together with Boswell's own admiration and impatience. It is the companion to Johnson's own account of the same tour and one of the founding texts of the literature of Scottish travel.
plot_or_argument: The journal follows the party from Edinburgh through St Andrews and Aberdeen to Inveraray, across to Skye and Mull and back by the west coast, noting what they saw and what Johnson said. The great subjects are the memory of the '45 and of the clan chiefs, the condition of the islanders, the debate over the Union and over the poverty of the islands, and Johnson's moral observations on the people he met, many of them at odds with Boswell's warmer sympathy. Boswell's own part - his devotion to Johnson, his flirtations, his pride in Scotland - is recorded as frankly as his companion's.
narrative_structure: A chronological day-by-day journal of a single tour, with continuous dialogue reported in the first person and no retrospectively imposed plot; the text prepared for 1785 retains the diary form.
principal_characters: James Boswell; Samuel Johnson; the chiefs and families of the islands; the old Jacobites of the West
literary_form: travel journal and autobiographical narrative, in the daily-notebook manner of Boswell's habit of recording
meter_and_prosody: Prose; plain, rapid and colloquial, with long passages of reported conversation and short topographical and antiquarian comment.
historical_context: Written in the season of the Highlands' touring vogue opened by Pennant and others, when the aftermath of the '45, the cleared estates and the debate over the Union made the western islands an argument about national character; publication in 1785 followed Johnson's own Journey of 1775 and the long delay caused by the political and personal delicacy of the material.
literary_significance: It is one of the most reliable documents of Johnson's spoken mind and one of the classic travel narratives of Scotland, and its representation of Highland and island life belongs to the literature of the nations in the age of Ossian and of the romantic tour. It also shows how the journal of a single tour became a mode of autobiographical realism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the journal was kept by Boswell in 1773 and revised for the press, and the date of the tour and the date of first publication are both firmly documented.
bibliographical_notes: The tour was made in 1773 and the Journal was first published in 1785; the standard text is that of the Yale edition, which records the manuscript and the printed versions of the narrative.

title: The Life of Samuel Johnson
alternative_titles: The Life of Samuel Johnson, LL.D.
Boswell's Life of Johnson
description: Boswell's biography of Johnson, the book that fixed the most familiar literary personality in English letters and invented the modern Life as an architecture of documents, conversation and chronology. It gathers letters, notebooks, the recollections of friends and Boswell's own journals into a year-by-year record of Johnson's studies, writings and company. It was advertised by a Prospectus of 1790 and published in 1791, with a revised second edition in 1793.
plot_or_argument: The Life follows Johnson from his birth at Lichfield, through his schooling, marriage, early poverty and labours at the Dictionary, to the years of the Idler, the Tour, the Pension and the last illness, with the conversations of the clubs and the clubs of friends filling the frame. Boswell reports Johnson's arguments on free-will, on death, on Scotland and on the Jacobite past at length, and permits the subject's inconsistencies to stand unharmonised. The result is a biography that is also a record of an age of letters, of the book trade and of opinion.
narrative_structure: A chronological biography with embedded documents - letters, certificates, earlier journals and the Tour - the largest continuous narrative being the years Boswell knew, and the whole prefaced by a statement of the materials and their provenance.
principal_characters: Samuel Johnson; James Boswell; Hester Lynch Thrale; Thomas Tyrwhitt; Joshua Reynolds; the club of the Mitre and the Turk's Head
literary_form: literary biography and memoir, combining chronicle, document transcription and reported conversation
meter_and_prosody: Prose; a plain chronological diction framing the reported speech, whose rhythm is carried by Johnson's own sentences as transcribed.
historical_context: Composed from materials assembled from Johnson's death in 1784 onward, in the decade when memoir and collected correspondence had become the standard mode of literary monument, and when the Scots and English literary worlds were being renegotiated after the American controversy. The work belongs with the late eighteenth-century efflorescence of biography and of the printed journal.
literary_significance: It is the foundational text of modern literary biography and the chief source for Johnson's mind and for the social history of Augustan and late-Augustan letters; its methods of transcription and chronology set the standard for later lives. It also preserves much of the periodical, critical and political writing of the age in a single narrative.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested for the whole, though the Life incorporates the letters and papers of many hands, and the abridgements and re-editings of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries have repeatedly altered its state; the modern standard edition restores the several layers of the text.
bibliographical_notes: The Life was published in 1791, printed by A. Strahan in London and by Charles Wilson in Edinburgh for Charles Dilly and George Wilkie; the Prospectus advertising the design had been issued in 1790, and a revised and enlarged second edition followed in 1793. The dates current in the bibliographies therefore refer to the Prospectus (1790), the first edition (1791) and the second edition (1793), and 1791 is entered here as the publication date of the first edition. The composition dates follow the assembly of the materials from Johnson's death in 1784 onward. The standard scholarly text is the multi-volume edition, and the six-volume Birkbeck Hill edition of 1887 remains the handy collected state.

title: Sermons (Hugh Blair)
description: The collected sermons of Blair, minister of St Giles's in Edinburgh and the most widely read Scottish preacher of his generation, issued from the later 1770s and reprinted across the English-speaking world. They exhibit the temperament of moderated Augustan pulpit oratory: practical, moral, polished, addressed to the feelings and to the conduct of ordinary life rather than to doctrinal controversy. Their success made Blair the standard model of the polite sermon and a central presence in the rhetoric of the Scottish Enlightenment.
plot_or_argument: The discourses take up the duties of the Christian life - the government of the passions, the duties of social and family conduct, the improvement of the mind, the conduct of affliction and the hope of a future state - and expound their texts with an orderly argument from observation of human feeling to practical application. Blair's handling of the parables and of the gospel history is narrative and affective, and his perorations press the auditor toward self-examination without invoking terrors.
narrative_structure: A serial volume of separately preached discourses, each a single argument with an opening explication of the text, a progression of reflections and a closing application; the several series were gathered in successive volumes.
literary_form: published pulpit oratory and practical divinity, in the polite sermon tradition of the eighteenth century
meter_and_prosody: Prose; the balanced period, the graduated triple, the measured cadence and the clear syllabic emphasis for which Blair's theory of elocution was written into his own practice.
historical_context: Preached and collected in the decades of Blair's incumbency at St Giles's and of his Edinburgh professorship of rhetoric and belles lettres, when the moderated Calvinism of the Scottish church and the culture of feeling met in the pulpit, and when the sermon was a literary genre with a substantial print market.
literary_significance: The Sermons were among the most reprinted religious books of the age, admired for their style by Blair's Scottish auditors and by the French and German translators who used them. They supply the practical counterpart to the Lectures on Rhetoric and remain the standard illustration of polite pulpit oratory in the culture of feeling.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the several series of Blair's Sermons appeared across the later eighteenth century and the volumes are documented by his own publication of them, so the date entered here is that of the first collected series, with the later volumes described in the note.
bibliographical_notes: The first collected series of the Sermons was issued in Edinburgh and London in 1777, with further volumes following in the subsequent years; the whole was widely reprinted and translated. The dates of the individual discourses are not fixed for every sermon, and the composition range entered is approximate.

title: Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres
description: The published substance of Blair's professorial course at Edinburgh, the first institutional chair of rhetoric and belles lettres in Britain, and the most influential textbook of taste and composition of its generation. It joins a theory of taste, a history of the styles of writing and an analysis of the genres - epic, tragedy, ode, satire, the periodical essay - with precepts on pronunciation and elocution. For half a century it was the standard manual of literary judgment in Britain and America.
plot_or_argument: The lectures begin with the principles of taste and with the sublime and the beautiful, proceed through the historical stages of literature and the study of the ancient and modern writers, and then examine the species of composition in prose and verse, the passions, the figures, the kinds of style and the rules of delivery. Blair argues that taste is founded on common sense and on the sympathy of mankind, that genius must be disciplined by rule and by the ancients, and that the criticism of a work must consult the sentiments and the manners of its own age.
narrative_structure: A course of lectures in three broad parts - the principles of taste and the history of literature, the species of composition with illustrative extracts and remarks, and elocution and delivery - each number a self-contained lesson with examples.
literary_form: critical treatise and professorial textbook, with anthologised extracts and commentaries
meter_and_prosody: Prose; clear, temperate and exemplary, written to be a model of the styles it prescribes, with the illustrative extracts supplying the metrical variety.
historical_context: Delivered after Blair's appointment to the new Edinburgh chair and published in 1783, in the full tide of the Scottish Enlightenment's analysis of taste, sympathy and the progress of the arts, and in the same years as the vogue of the fine arts and of the history of literature. Its use in universities and academies made it a vehicle of the period's educational programme.
literary_significance: It codified the century's criticism of taste, sublimity and genre into a teachable system and became the grammar of literary judgment for the nineteenth century, for readers and for institutions on both sides of the Atlantic. Its treatment of primitive and national poetry, of the sublime and of elocution also makes it an index to the movements of taste that produced the graveyard and the ballad revivals.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the lectures are those of Blair's course at Edinburgh, and the printed edition was prepared by him from the matter used in teaching, with several later editions revised.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1783 in two volumes at Edinburgh and London, and reprinted and abridged very frequently through the nineteenth century, with translations into several European languages; the text is standardly read from facsimiles of the first edition and from the studies of Blair's criticism.

title: The Grave (Hugh Blair)
description: The sermon on death and the grave that made Blair's reputation while he was still a young minister in Carrick, and one of the most quoted pieces of Scottish pulpit prose of the mid-century. Preached at Colmonell and published at Edinburgh in 1743, it meditates on the burial place, the bodies of the dead and the terrors and consolations of the last hour, and passes from the spectacle of the grave to the hope of the resurrection. It belongs with the graveyard verse of the same decades as an expression of the new taste for solemn meditation.
plot_or_argument: Blair leads his auditors to the graveyard and holds before them the equality of the dead, the silence of the tomb and the uncertainty of the hour of death, pressing each hearer to imagine himself laid there. He then turns the meditation upon the resurrection and the judgment, so that the terrors of the grave are answered by a reasoned hope. The argument moves by description and appeal rather than by doctrine, and its aim is the reformation of present conduct through the continual thought of death.
narrative_structure: A single preached discourse moving from the meditation on the grave and the dead, through the contemplation of mortality and judgment, to the consolation of the resurrection and the practical application.
literary_form: published sermon and graveyard meditation, in the solemn descriptive manner of the mid-century
meter_and_prosody: Prose; deliberately sonorous and cadenced, with the balanced period, the pause and the climax of the elocutionary school that Blair later theorised.
historical_context: Preached and issued in the tradition of graveyard meditation opened by Parnell's night piece and by Edward Young's Night Thoughts, and some years before Robert Blair's poem of the same name; it belongs to the religious atmosphere of the Scottish west before the Moderate ascendancy, and its success marked the arrival of a new taste for the awful and the pathetic in Scottish discourse.
literary_significance: It is the classical prose statement of the graveyard meditation and helped to fix the rhetoric of solemnity in Scottish preaching for a generation. It also supplies the link between sermon and poem in the preromantic interest in death, and its reputation was long maintained by its place in collections of elocution.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the sermon's publication at Edinburgh in 1743 is given in the usual bibliographical reckoning, and the later enlarged editions are Blair's own revision.
bibliographical_notes: Published at Edinburgh in 1743 and frequently reprinted, enlarged and translated, and long kept in view through the elocutionary and anthology traditions; the precise date of the discourse as preached is not fixed here, so the composition start is left null.

title: Poems on Several Occasions (Warton)
alternative_titles: The Poems on Several Occasions of Thomas Warton
description: Thomas Warton's first volume, published while he was still at Oxford and the book that announced the revival of the English ode and of the imaginative romance tradition. It gathers the Pindaric odes, the translations, the lyric and descriptive pieces and the pieces in the old romantic measures, together with the early critical essay on Pope's genius. The volume is the opening statement of the Warton programme: a history of English taste joined to the practice of imaginative verse.
plot_or_argument: The odes attempt the irregular Pindaric forms on subjects of contemplation, fancy and moral description, while the lyric pieces cultivate melancholy, retirement and the observation of landscape. The critical essay measures Pope's art against the older English poets and argues for a wider and more historical sense of poetical excellence. The whole volume moves between imitation of the ancients, experiment in the native measures, and antiquarian curiosity about the romance tradition.
narrative_structure: A collected volume of separate poems ordered by class, with the odes, the translations and the descriptive pieces distributed across the book and the critical essay printed as an early separate performance gathered into it.
principal_characters: The personified Fancy and Melancholy of the odes; the contemplative speakers of the descriptive pieces; Pope, as the subject of the critical essay
literary_form: collected odes, lyrics, translations and occasional verse, in the Pindaric and preromantic manner
meter_and_prosody: Irregular Pindaric stanzas of long and short lines after the manner of Dryden and Oldham, together with smooth heroic couplets for the descriptive and critical pieces.
historical_context: Published in 1746 from Oxford, in the season of the ode vogue and of the revival of interest in Spenser and in the old English romance, and in the intellectual circle of his brother Joseph Warton and of the Oxford critics who were revaluing imaginative poetry against Augustan rule.
literary_significance: The volume is one of the founding documents of the preromantic and Gothic revival in English verse, and its Pindaric experiments, with those of Mason and Gray, prepared the way for the Romantic ode. Its mixture of verse and literary-historical criticism marks the movement from Augustan taste to the history of taste.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume belongs to Thomas Warton the younger, poet laureate from 1785, and must be distinguished from the poems of Joseph Warton and from the later collected editions in which pieces were added and withdrawn.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1746 and reissued in enlarged form in the later editions of Warton's poems, with pieces of uncertain first dating; the essay on Pope had appeared separately in the mid-1740s and was gathered into the volume. The date of composition of the individual poems varies across the 1740s, and the range entered is approximate.

title: Observations on the Faerie Queene of Spenser
alternative_titles: Observations on the Faerie Queene of the Glorious Poet Ed. Spenser
description: Warton's scholarly edition of and commentary on Spenser's poem, the work that revived the heroic allegory in the age of the rules and made Spenser a classic again. Its observations explain the obsolete language, the allegory, the sources and the romances that Spenser used, and its preliminary dissertation argues for the historical dignity of the native tradition of chivalric poem. The book is a foundation of English literary scholarship and of the Gothic revival.
plot_or_argument: The commentary expounds the allegorical persons and the moral and political design of Spenser's fable, traces his imitation of earlier romance and of the Italian poets, and glosses the archaic vocabulary with the help of the old writers. The prefatory matter argues that the genius of Spenser belongs to a national tradition of allegory and chivalry which the false taste of later ages had neglected, and that the poet's allegory must be read historically as well as morally. Together the observations establish the method of editing a native classic by the evidence of its own age.
narrative_structure: An edition with preliminary dissertation and continuous annotation, the commentary arranged by book and stanza of the poem it illustrates rather than as a free-standing argument.
principal_characters: Spenser; the allegorical persons of the Faerie Queene; the romancers and Italian poets named as sources
literary_form: scholarly annotation and critical dissertation; editorial commentary on a native classic
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the notes and dissertation, the Spenserian stanza of the edited poem being the object of the historical account of metre.
historical_context: Published in 1754, in the season of the revived esteem for Spenser among the Oxford and London wits and of the debate about the allegorical romance, and alongside the antiquarian work on chivalry and the British poetic tradition that Warton's own History of English Poetry later completed.
literary_significance: It created the modern scholarly study of Spenser and supplied the model of historical annotation for English poets, influencing the editorial practice of the later eighteenth century. Its defence of allegory and romance is a central document of the Gothic and antiquarian revival and of the transfer of taste from the rules to national literary history.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is Thomas Warton's, and the date of its composition before publication is not fixed for every part, so the composition start is left null.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1754 in two volumes, with a second edition appearing later in the century; the dissertation and annotations were revised, and the standard account of the book is in the histories of Spenserian scholarship and of Warton's career.

title: The History of English Poetry
alternative_titles: The History of English Poetry, from the Close of the Eleventh Century to the Commencement of the Eighteenth Century
description: Warton's great unfinished scholarly history, the first attempt to trace the whole course of English poetry from the medieval minstrels to the Augustan age and to explain it by the manners, learning and opinions of each period. Its four volumes set the model of historical literary criticism in English and made the romance, the chivalric lays and the early drama part of a continuous national story. The work is at once a history of letters and an argument for the imaginative tradition that the age of rule had disparaged.
plot_or_argument: The history follows the poets in their social and intellectual conditions, beginning with the remains of ancient poetry and the minstrel and romantic lays, and moving through the allegorical and chivalric tradition, the rise of the drama, the Spenserians, and the ages of the civil war and of the Restoration. Its great digressions treat the origin and progress of romance and chivalry, the origin of the ancient epick poems, and the rise of the drama, each a piece of general literary history. The method throughout is antiquarian: to recover the documents, the manners and the beliefs from which the poems were made.
narrative_structure: A multi-volume literary history arranged chronologically with long embedded dissertations or digressions on general subjects; the volumes were issued successively and the fourth was published after the earlier three, with materials left imperfect.
principal_characters: The medieval minstrels and romancers; Chaucer; Spenser; the Elizabethan dramatists; the poets of the Restoration and of the Augustan age
literary_form: literary history and critical scholarship, in the new historical method of letters
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the narrative and dissertations, the metrical specimens quoted being the objects of historical and prosodic comment rather than of verse composition.
historical_context: Issued volume by volume from 1774 to 1781, in the decades of antiquarian recovery, of the Ossianic debate over primitive poetry and of the growing claim that the imagination, not the rule, was the poetical faculty; it belongs with Percy's and Evans's collections and with the revival of the early drama as a single movement of taste.
literary_significance: It founded the historical study of English poetry and supplied the framework within which later romantic and Victorian scholars read their own tradition. Its account of chivalry, allegory and romance made the native medieval past available as literary history, and its method established the digression as a vehicle of general criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the successive volumes and their imperfect completion are documented in Warton's own correspondence and in the later biographies, and the volume sequence is recorded in the note below.
bibliographical_notes: The first two volumes appeared in 1774, the third in 1778 and the fourth in 1781, published in London; the work was long left without a complete scholarly text and the standard modern account is in the histories of literary scholarship, with the individual volumes still read from the first editions.

title: Poems on Several Occasions (Barbauld)
alternative_titles: The Poems on Several Occasions of Anna Letitia Barbauld
description: Anna Laetitia Barbauld's first volume of verse, published in 1773 when she was still Anna Aikin and the book that opened one of the most considerable literary careers of the later century. It contains the early odes, hymns and elegies, the familiar epistles to friends, and the pieces on retirement, on the pleasures of the imagination and on the duties of feeling. Its manner unites the eighteenth-century ode tradition with a new intimacy of domestic and moral observation.
plot_or_argument: The poems argue for a poetry of sensibility and of religious feeling, addressing friendship, solitude, the death of the young and the consolation of the mind in retirement. The epistles cultivate the conversational line of the native school, praising a circle of friends and the pleasures of study and home, while the odes and hymns attempt the higher imaginative forms after the manner of the age. Throughout, the volume claims for women's writing a serious place in the moral and devotional registers.
narrative_structure: A collected volume of separate poems ordered by class, with the odes and hymns, the elegies and the familiar epistles distributed through the book; later editions were enlarged.
principal_characters: The friends and correspondents of the epistles; the mourner and the child of the elegies; the personified pleasures and powers of the odes
literary_form: collected odes, hymns, elegies and familiar verse epistles in the school of feeling
meter_and_prosody: The irregular ode and hymn stanzas of the eighteenth-century manner, with smooth heroic couplets and four-beat elegiac measures in the familiar pieces.
historical_context: Published in 1773 in the circle of the Newington Green and Worcester nonconformist intelligentsia surrounding her father the Rev. John Aikin and her husband the Rev. John Aikin Barbauld, and in the years when the ode, the hymn and the domestic epistle were the living forms of dissenting and sentimental verse.
literary_significance: The volume established the voice that later made Barbauld the central writer for children and one of the most formidable critics and pamphleteers of the 1790s. Its handling of sensibility, devotion and friendship makes it a key text of women's writing in the culture of feeling and of the dissenting poetic tradition.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the early volume is entered in the standard bibliographies under her maiden and married names, and the pieces were composed across the years before publication, so the composition range is approximate.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1773 and reissued in enlarged form in the collected Poems of 1789 and later editions; the dating of individual pieces varies and is recorded in the scholarly studies of her work.

title: The Pleasures of Memory
alternative_titles: The Pleasures of Memory. A Novel
description: Barbauld's first prose work, a moral tale of sensibility in two volumes which takes its title and its method from the theory of memory as a source of pleasure and of virtue. It follows a young heroine of principle through dependence, courtship and the trials of family interest, and makes the recollection of past affection the ground of her conduct. The book belongs with the domestic and educational fiction of the 1770s and was repeatedly reprinted.
plot_or_argument: The story sets a virtuous young woman against the importunities of interest, flattery and worldly alliance, and resolves the trials of fortune by the constancy of affection and by the moral uses of remembrance. The narrative dwells on home, on the society of good minds and on the pleasures which the memory draws from former scenes of kindness, and it argues that feeling rightly governed is the basis of duty. Its conclusion rewards principle and exposes the claims of rank and money as the false scales of merit.
narrative_structure: A novel of character and sentiment in two volumes, proceeding by domestic episodes and reported conversation, with the moral reflection of the title sustained as the principle of selection and of judgment.
literary_form: sentimental and domestic novel in the lineage of Richardson and of the conduct tale
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative with letters and dialogue; the style is reflective, balanced and addressed to the feelings rather than to incident.
historical_context: Published in 1776, in the vogue of the moral and sentimental novel and of the educational tale, and in the same nonconformist intellectual circle that produced her poems and, later, the children's books and the essays written with her brother . Its argument about memory and virtue draws on the associationist psychology then current.
literary_significance: It is the earliest evidence of Barbauld's power to put moral philosophy into narrative and a document of the culture of feeling as practised by women writers of the 1770s. Its concern with memory, affection and education anticipates Lessons for Children and the prose hymns, and its success helped to establish her livelihood by letters.
attribution_notes: Attribution rests on the standard bibliographies and on her family and biographical record; the novel was published anonymously, and the date of composition is not fixed, so the composition start is left null.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1776 in two volumes and reprinted in the following decades, sometimes with the other early prose of its author; the biographical and bibliographical studies of Barbauld record the several editions. The title should not be confused with Akenside's poem on the pleasures of imagination.

title: Lessons for Children
description: Barbauld's elementary books for the very young, begun in 1778 and issued in graduated classes, the first widely successful example in English of a reading course calculated for the mind of a child. The lessons move from single words and short dialogues about the household, the animals and the weather to longer narrative and moral pieces as the child's capacity grows. Their method of steady progression, of the familiar object and of the question-and-answer dialogue made them the model of children's teaching books for a century.
plot_or_argument: The earliest classes consist of short exchanges about things within a child's reach, naming, seeing and doing, and pass by easy steps to little stories and to the plainest duties of kindness, truthfulness and attention. Later classes introduce narrative, fable and reflection, still pitched to the child's experience and governed by the principle that instruction should follow the interests of the learner. The whole proceeds on the conviction that the mind of a child is to be led, not driven, and that pleasure is the proper engine of learning.
narrative_structure: A graded series of short lessons in several classes or parts, each rising in difficulty, arranged for sequential use rather than as a continuous story.
principal_characters: The child addressed; the instructing voice of the book; the household and animal figures of the dialogues
literary_form: children's educational prose and verse, in the graduated reading-lesson tradition
meter_and_prosody: Plain short sentences and dialogue in the earliest classes, with simple rhymed and rhythmic pieces introduced as the series proceeds.
historical_context: Written in the train of Locke's thinking on education and of the new interest in the education of infancy, and in the practical context of Barbauld's own teaching circle and of the nonconformist academies; the books belong to the 1770s revolution in the literature made for children, which treated the child as a reader with rights of its own.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of English literature written for the nursery and the direct ancestor of the progressive reading series, and it changed expectations of what a child could be given to read. Its doctrine of instruction through pleasure and familiar objects became orthodoxy in elementary education and in children's writing.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the classes appeared successively from 1778 and the dates of the several parts differ, so the composition start is left null with the series described in the note.
bibliographical_notes: The first class was published in 1778 and the following classes in the succeeding years, each part being titled for an age; there were many reprints and imitations throughout the nineteenth century, and the several parts and their dates are recorded in the histories of children's literature and in the studies of Barbauld's work.

title: Hymns in Prose for Children
description: Barbauld's devotional prose for the young, published in 1781 and designed to teach a child to address the Deity through the visible world. Each hymn takes some part of creation - the morning, the seasons, the insect and the elements, the breath of life - and turns its observation into praise, so that natural knowledge becomes the school of piety. The book is the most original religious writing of its author's middle period and one of the enduring children's texts of the century.
plot_or_argument: The hymns proceed by address and by observation of nature, leading the child from the creature and the scene to the attributes of the Creator, and from the gifts of the earth to the duties of gratitude, gentleness and truth. They insist that the Divine presence is to be found in every part of the world, and that praise is the proper employment of a mind that has learned to look. Their moral teaching is of benevolence extended to animals and to other men, and their religious temper is a reasoned and affectionate deism rather than a doctrine of terror.
narrative_structure: A series of short prose hymns, each a single meditation on an aspect of creation followed by ascription and petition, arranged for reading aloud with a child.
principal_characters: The child addressed; the speaking instructor; the creatures and elements of the meditations
literary_form: prose hymn and devotional writing for children, in the dissenting hymn tradition renewed in prose
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmed prose of short clauses and balanced address, pitched for recitation, with the cadences of prayer and of the hymn preserved without verse.
historical_context: Published in 1781 alongside the elementary books that had made Barbauld's name in education, in a period when the hymn and the prose devotional were being addressed to children as never before, and within a Unitarian and dissenting culture that preferred rational piety to the language of dread.
literary_significance: It created the model of nature as a book of praise for the child reader and influenced both religious instruction and the nature-writing tradition of the nineteenth century. Its combination of sensibility, natural history and devotion makes it a central document of the culture of feeling applied to education.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was published under the author's name as the writer of her elementary books, and the date of composition is not separately fixed, so the composition start is left null.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1781 and frequently reprinted, often bound with her other elementary books; the standard account of the text and its editions is in the studies of Barbauld's works for children.
